novel_idea.topic_thesis: Reversibility is temporary: once an AI workflow is embedded in roles, metrics, training, and doctrine, the organization—not the model—becomes the lock-in.
novel_idea.angle: Use the delayed productivity gains from electrification to show why technically reversible AI pilots can become organizationally irreversible long before leaders recognize the underlying architecture as wrong.
novel_idea.hook: The dangerous AI decision is not choosing the wrong model. It is training the organization around a temporary workflow.
novel_idea.argument_summary: Electrification produced its largest gains only after factories redesigned complementary systems such as layouts, accounting, management practices, and operating concepts. Those complements also made each architecture durable and costly to replace. AI creates the same path-dependence: a model or agent can be swapped quickly, but the surrounding roles, measures, interfaces, habits, and doctrine cannot. As those complements accumulate, an apparently reversible pilot hardens into organizational capital. Operators should therefore evaluate reversibility at the level of the whole work system and resist institutionalizing an agent architecture before it has survived real boundary-of-consequence feedback. This differs from the prior argument that reversibility lowers the social cost of criticism: the new claim is that reversibility itself decays as organizational complements accumulate.
novel_idea.novelty_rationale: The closest post argues that breaking a plan into reversible pieces makes criticism cheaper and honesty safer. This argument identifies a different causal mechanism and operator problem: sunk investment, trained habits, and complementary organizational systems progressively eliminate reversibility. The consequence is not primarily better candor but avoidance of path-dependent AI architecture lock-in. The operator decision also changes from structuring reversible experiments to delaying institutional hardening and testing reversibility across the entire work system.
novel_idea.source_grounding: The source’s electrification discussion says productivity gains lagged while complementary layouts, accounting systems, management practices, and operating concepts developed. The Paul David material adds that incumbents preserved durable capital rationally, that transitions are path-dependent, and that early commitment to an agent doctrine, interface, or work shape can lock a firm through sunk investment and trained habits. It explicitly describes the organizational chart as durable capital and warns that replacement is costly and partly irreversible.

payload.body_text:
The dangerous AI pilot is not the one that fails. It’s the one that works just well enough to reorganize the company around it.

Paul David showed why electrification took decades to lift productivity. Early factories replaced steam engines with dynamos but kept the old line shafts, belts, and layouts. The real gains came only after factories were rebuilt around distributed electric motors.

AI pilots look reversible because models and APIs can be swapped. But then owners are assigned, roles change, metrics harden, training spreads, and approval chains adapt. The model remains replaceable. The organization does not.

By the time leaders discover the workflow encoded the wrong architecture, rollback means unwinding status, incentives, skills, and promises. That is no longer a technical decision. It is an institutional fight.

Treat every AI pilot as an architecture decision. Design the deletion path before adoption creates a constituency.
